docs.text: Runtime extensions (spec v2) The original pages describe the JSON as first designed. The walk-around multiplayer runtime needs a few things those pages do not cover: where avatars can walk, where they appear, how scenes connect, where items and characters stand, and which state is shared between players. Everything on this page is optional and additive . A document that uses none of it still plays: the whole scene is walkable, players appear in the centre, and all variables are per-player. Set "spec_version": 2 on scenarios that use these fields. All coordinates are scene pixels with the origin at the top left. An avatar's position is the position of its feet . Scenario Parameter Type Default Description spec_version int 1 Version of the spec the document was written against. code string The scenario's unique 16-letter code (lowercase a to z ). It is generated when the scenario is created, never changes, and is its address: players open /{code} . shortname stays as a readable name and can be edited freely. items array Item definitions (see Items ). Scenes place them with scenes[].items . characters array Character definitions (see Characters ). Scenes place them with scenes[].characters . asset_base_url string Prefix for media url values that are neither absolute nor rooted. A url that starts with / (such as /media/12/ab12….png , a file uploaded in the editor) is used as it is. visibility string public public : on every player's missions page. private : only for students a teacher assigned it to. chat_mode string emotes off : no chat. emotes : a fixed set of emoji only. free : typed text, filtered by the game server. move_speed decimal 420 Avatar walking speed in scene pixels per second. avatar_media_ids array Image media ids players may choose as their avatar. The first is the default. With the Laravel API these are the platform's avatars, the same in every scenario, added when the document is served (media ids from 900000); a scenario does not set them. See Classes, missions and teams . avatar_portraits object A close-up portrait for an avatar: {"": } . Shown when a player with that avatar speaks in a story box. An avatar without one is shown by its ordinary picture. objectives array The mission checklist shown to the player. See below. music_media_id int Background music for the scenario: it plays in every scene that does not have music of its own. music_volume decimal 0.5 Volume of that music, 0 to 1. session object null Save data for the requesting player. See Save data . jump_targets is generated from jump actions (including those on infobox buttons), by the API when it builds the JSON and again by the runtime. It may be either an object keyed by scene id ( {"3": [4]} ) or an array of {scene_id, targets} . The game server only lets a player move to a scene listed in the current scene's jump targets. Objectives A scenario can define a checklist that is shown on screen while it is played. Objectives are driven by variables, so events move the mission along simply by changing variables. Parameter Type Default Description id string or int Unique within the scenario. text string What the player reads. May contain placeholders, e.g. Collect samples ({{samples}}/3) . show_when array of conditions always The objective is listed only while these hold. Use it to reveal steps as the mission unfolds. complete_when array of conditions The objective is ticked while these hold. Required. optional bool false Shown as a bonus. The player is told when an objective becomes complete. Placeholders in text Text overlays, infobox content, infobox button labels, text labels and objective text may contain placeholders: {{variable_name}} is replaced with the variable's current value. Reserved variables work too. {{media:ID}} is replaced with the URL of a media asset, for use in infobox HTML: . Values are escaped when inserted into HTML. A placeholder that names nothing is left as written, so a typo shows up. Scenes Parameter Type Default Description width, height int first background's size World size in pixels. Set these : the game server cannot see image files, and uses the size to check movement. walkable_areas array of polygons whole scene Where feet may be. A polygon is an array of {x, y} points. A point is walkable if it is inside any of them. blocked_areas array of polygons Holes cut out of the walkable areas (furniture, pits). spawn_points array Named places players appear. See below. items array Item placements: {item_id, position_x, position_y} . characters array Character placements: {character_id, position_x, position_y, facing, event_id} . indirect_events array Events that only run via a run event action, an infobox button or a character. (Mentioned on the Events page; this is where they live.) Background and foreground layers Entries of background_media and foreground_media may be plain media objects, as before, or layer objects: Parameter Type Default Description media_id int Media to draw. position_x, position_y decimal 0 Top-left corner. display_width, display_height decimal scene size Size to draw the image at. tile bool false Repeat the image to fill the display size. scroll_speed_x, scroll_speed_y decimal 0 For tiled layers: pixels per second the texture drifts. parallax decimal 1 Camera scroll factor. 1 moves with the world, 0 stays fixed on screen. Backgrounds draw in order behind everything; foregrounds draw in order in front of avatars. Background music A scene starts with its own music ( music_media_id , music_volume on the scene) or, failing that, the scenario's. Events can change the music at any time with an audio action flagged repeat and persist ; the next scene starts with its own music again. One music track plays at a time, and a track that is already playing is never restarted, so walking between scenes that share music is seamless. A scene whose start events start background music themselves is left to do so. Scale areas scale_areas is a list of boxes that give a scene depth. Whatever stands in a box is drawn at scale_top percent of its normal size at the box's top edge and scale_bottom percent at its bottom edge, and in proportion in between. It applies to avatars, to what they wear or ride, and to items and characters, by where their feet are. Parameter Type Description name string A label for the editor. x, y, width, height int The box, in scene pixels. scale_top decimal Percent of normal size at the top edge. 100 is unchanged. scale_bottom decimal Percent of normal size at the bottom edge. speed_effect decimal How much walking speed follows size, 0 to 100. Default 100: one to one, so a figure drawn at half size walks at half speed. 0: speed is unaffected. A value such as 60 lets distant figures cover ground a little faster than their size suggests without looking like they are racing. "scale_areas": [{ "name": "corridor depth", "x": 0, "y": 580, "width": 1800, "height": 620, "scale_top": 40, "scale_bottom": 100 }] Scale areas are separate from walkable areas on purpose: a crate at the far end of a room should be small even though nobody can walk there. Outside every box things are drawn at normal size. Where boxes overlap, the first one listed applies. Scale areas change how things are drawn and, through speed_effect , how fast avatars walk. Hotspot radii, reach and blocking radii stay in scene pixels. The game server's speed limit is the full walking speed, so slowing down in a scale area never conflicts with it. Spawn points Parameter Type Default Description name string Unique within the scene. The one named default is used when none is asked for. position_x, position_y decimal facing string right left or right . Moving between scenes Scenes are connected the way the original docs describe: with jump actions . To send players to the next scene when they reach the edge of the current one, put a walk-in hotspot along that edge and give it a jump action. A hotspot whose position_x or position_y is null covers that entire axis, so one hotspot makes a whole edge: { "id": 310, "shortname": "edge-east", "position_x": 2250, "position_y": null, "radius": 35, "activate_by_trigger": false, "actions": [{ "id": 3101, "type": "jump", "scene_id": 4, "spawn_point": "west" }] } This fires when an avatar comes within 35 pixels of x = 2250, at any height. Use position_y with a null position_x for a top or bottom edge. Because it is an ordinary hotspot it can have conditions (a locked door), and the jump can be preceded by other actions (a sound, a line of text). The scene's end events run before the jump, as always. The spawn point a jump arrives at must not be inside a walk-in hotspot that jumps, or arriving players would leave again at once. The validator rejects this. Events and hotspots activate_by_trigger keeps its meaning. In a walk-around game the two cases are: true : fires when the player clicks or taps inside the radius (or on one of the hotspot's labels). false : fires when the player's avatar walks into the radius. It fires again each time they leave and re-enter. If it cannot fire at that moment (another event is blocking hotspots, or its conditions are not met) it fires as soon as it can while the avatar is still inside. Parameter Type Default Description once bool false Fire only once per player, ever. Remembered in the save data. reveal_radius decimal The hotspot is only there when the player's avatar is within this many scene pixels of its position. Further away, its labels are invisible and it cannot be clicked. Absent: it is always there. reveal_full_radius decimal half of reveal_radius Within this distance the hotspot is fully visible. Between the two distances its labels fade in as the avatar approaches and out as it leaves. The reveal distance is measured from each player's own avatar, so a hotspot can be visible to one player and not yet to another. A coordinate the hotspot leaves empty does not count towards the distance. Walk-in hotspots still fire by their radius alone. Who sees an event Parameter Type Default Description audience string player player : only the player who sets the event off sees it. scene : every player in the scene sees and hears it as it happens. Every kind of event can have an audience . With scene , these actions are shown to the other players in the scene at the moment they happen for the player who set the event off: audio , image_fixed , image_overlay , text_overlay , spritemap , video , dialogue , translate and cancel . In a shared dialogue, "the player" is the player who set it off: the bubble hangs over their avatar, and a story box shows their name and portrait. Everything an event does stays with the player who set it off, whatever the audience: variable , award , jump , freeze , avatar , shop , infobox and the timing actions. Nothing another player's event shows can change your variables, move you or open a box you must answer. (A variable that should change for everyone is a shared variable; see Variables . An avatar being hidden is seen by everyone anyway.) The player's own conditions decide which actions run; the others are shown exactly those. A player who walks into the scene part-way through sees the rest, not what came before. For something that must still be true for late arrivals (the boulders are across the path), use a shared variable and a hotspot or start event conditioned on it; use audience: scene for the moment itself (the boulders falling). An event run with run_event has its own audience: a private conversation can set off a shared event. The game server passes on only actions that belong to a scene event in the scene the player is in, so a player cannot push anything else onto other screens. { "id": 553, "shortname": "rockfall", "audience": "scene", "actions": [ { "type": "text_overlay", "text": "RUMBLE! Boulders crash down across the cliff path.", "duration": 3000, "blocking": false }, { "type": "variable", "name": "rockfall", "operator": "set", "operand": 1 } ] } overridable is implemented as: when any event starts, every running event flagged overridable is stopped where it is. Events not flagged always run to the end. Actions Action type values are matched loosely: Image Fixed , imageFixed and image_fixed are the same. The canonical names are audio , cancel , image_fixed , image_overlay , infobox , jump , repeat , run_event , spritemap , text_overlay , translate , variable , video and wait . Actions may carry their own conditions array (the Conditions page allows this; the Actions page did not list it). An action whose conditions fail is skipped. Dialogue A new action type, dialogue , shows what someone says: in a speech bubble over them, or in a story box with their portrait. Parameter Type Default Description text string What is said. {{variable}} placeholders work. speaker string player player , or character . character_id int The character, when speaker is character . For a bubble it must be placed in the scene; a story box can carry a voice from anywhere. style string bubble bubble : a speech bubble over the speaker. portrait : a story box. duration int Milliseconds on screen. Absent: a bubble stays long enough to read, and a story box stays until the player continues. A click closes either sooner. { "type": "dialogue", "speaker": "character", "character_id": 1, "text": "Welcome aboard, {{QuestLabPlayerName}}!" } The bubble follows the speaker and keeps itself on screen. It sits above them when there is room, below when they are near the top of the screen, and to the right or left when there is room neither above nor below; sideways it slides along to stay inside the screen while its tail keeps pointing at the speaker. A sequence of dialogue actions is a conversation; put a freeze before it to hold the player still. The story box ( style: "portrait" ) is for the characters and moments that carry the story. It is a panel across the bottom of the screen with the speaker's close-up portrait standing on its edge, their name, and the words appearing a few at a time. The player clicks, or presses Enter or Space, to continue: once to show the whole line, again to go on. The portrait is the character's portrait_media_id (or their ordinary picture), or for the player the portrait of their avatar ( avatar_portraits ). { "type": "dialogue", "style": "portrait", "speaker": "character", "character_id": 1, "text": "Welcome aboard, {{QuestLabPlayerName}}! I am Captain Vega." } A story conversation is normally the player's own ( audience: player , the default), as the captain's greeting in the demo is. If its event is shown to the scene, the other players get a smaller version at the top of the screen that closes by itself and never takes their clicks or keys. Animate A new action type, animate , plays an animation on something in the scene. See Animations for where animations come from. Parameter Type Default Description animation string The animation's name: one defined on the target's sprite sheet, or a built-in move ( jump , spin , crouch , wave , dance ). Empty: stop what is playing and return to standing and walking. target string player player : the avatar of the player whose event this is. item : an item or vehicle, on the floor of this scene or being worn or ridden. character : a character placed in this scene. action : a picture that an image_fixed action is showing. item_id, character_id, target_id int Which item, character or action, for those targets. { "type": "animate", "target": "character", "character_id": 1, "animation": "wave", "blocking": false } With blocking (the default) the sequence waits until a one-pass animation has finished; a looping one never holds it up. An animation on a player's avatar goes through the game server , so everyone in the scene sees it, whatever the event's audience. An animation on an item, a character or a picture is shown to the other players only when the event's audience is scene , like anything else an event shows. Freeze A new action type, freeze , stops the player from walking, or lets them walk again: for a conversation with a character, a cutscene, a countdown. Parameter Type Description frozen bool true : the player cannot move. false : they can again. { "type": "freeze", "frozen": true } A freeze ends at a freeze action with frozen: false , or when the event that froze the player finishes , or on leaving the scene, whichever comes first, so a player can never be left stuck by a missing action. While frozen a player can still click hotspots and infobox buttons. The demo freezes the player while Captain Vega is speaking. Avatar A new action type, avatar , shows or hides the player's own avatar. Parameter Type Default Description visible bool false hides the avatar, true shows it. duration int 0 Fade time in milliseconds. { "type": "avatar", "visible": false, "duration": 400 } The change goes through the game server, so every player in the scene sees it. A hidden player can still walk and use hotspots. Avatars are always shown again when a player arrives in a scene : to keep them hidden in a scene, hide them in one of its start events. The demo's rocket hides the avatar as the player steps aboard, and the player reappears in the control room. (The scene attribute show_avatars: false from the base docs still hides every avatar in a scene, for everyone, for the whole visit.) Award A new action type, award , gives the player stars, XP, or both. A negative number takes them away. Parameter Type Default Description stars int 0 Stars to give (or take, if negative). Stars are the currency of the marketplace. xp int 0 Experience points to give (or take). XP is never spent; it adds up to a rank. note string A few words shown with the award: "Sample collected". repeatable bool false By default a player gets each award once , however often its event runs and in however many visits. Set this to give it every time. { "type": "award", "stars": 3, "xp": 10, "note": "Sample collected" } Stars and XP belong to the player's account , not to a scenario: they carry across every scenario on the platform. See Stars, XP and the marketplace for how they are kept honest. Neither total goes below zero. Taking away more than a player has leaves them with none. Guests earn nothing. Stars and XP need a signed-in account. Put awards in an event's own actions. An award placed directly on an infobox button is not given (the validator warns): make the button run an event ( run_event ) that contains the award. Awards never hold up the sequence, whatever blocking says. Shop A new action type, shop , opens the marketplace. It has no parameters. The sequence waits until the player closes the window. { "type": "shop" } Players can also open the marketplace at any time from the stars shown in the corner of the screen, so a scenario needs no shop action; it is there for scenarios that want a place for it, as the demo's marketplace room does. Addition Applies to Description dismissible infobox Default true. See below. spawn_point jump Spawn point to arrive at in the target scene. target_event_id run_event The event to run. Use this rather than event_id , which the base action attributes already use for "the event this action belongs to". event_id is still read if target_event_id is absent. layer image_fixed, spritemap above (default) draws over avatars and foregrounds. sorted depth-sorts with avatars using position_y , so players can walk in front of it. position_x, position_y, scale_x, scale_y, alpha, duration translate Values present are animated on the target over duration milliseconds. Position applies to image_fixed and spritemap targets; overlays support scale and alpha. alignment, scale_x, scale_y, volume video Video plays as an overlay with browser controls. It blocks until it ends. Clarifications of documented behaviour: An action with no end (an image or text with duration 0, repeating audio, a repeating spritemap) never holds up the sequence, whatever blocking says. It stays until a cancel or a jump. A repeat with no wait in its loop runs about once per frame rather than freezing the page. call_to_actions is a list of {"text": "...", "action": {...}, "conditions": [...]} . The action needs no id . A button with conditions is only offered while they hold, so one infobox can serve as a menu that changes. An infobox has a close button unless dismissible is false . A box that cannot be dismissed must be answered with one of its buttons, which is how questions are asked. An infobox action is not finished until the box is closed and the chosen button's action has run to its end. A sequence such as "ask a question, then open a menu" therefore waits for the feedback the answer triggers. Infobox content is sanitised. Formatting, lists, tables, links and images are kept; scripts, styles, frames and event handlers are removed. Background music is an audio action with repeat and persist in a scene's start events. Persistent audio is treated as the music track: only one plays at a time. When a scene starts a persistent audio action with the same media that is already playing, the music carries on without restarting; with different media, it replaces the old track. A cancel action naming the audio action's id stops it. Variables Parameter Type Default Description scope string player player : each player has their own value, saved with their progress. room : one value shared by everyone in the group, held by the game server. persist bool true If false the variable returns to default_value on every visit. Each variable is one or the other, and its scope says which. A player's own variable ( player ) has a separate value for every player. Changing it for one player changes nothing for anyone else. Use it for a player's progress: students must greet three animals before a door opens, and each has their own count of how many they have greeted. A shared variable ( room ) has one value for everyone playing together. When any player changes it, it changes for all of them at once, wherever in the scenario they are. Use it for the state of the world: one student sends boulders down across a path, and after that nobody can use the path. Conditions and variable actions are written the same way for both; only the variable's scope differs, so a scenario decides this once, where the variable is defined, and not in every action. A variable action on a shared variable is sent to the game server, applied there, and the new value reaches every player; hotspots and objectives whose conditions use it update for everyone. The editor marks shared variables wherever one is chosen. "Everyone playing together" is a group: the players who joined with the same group key (a class, a team), up to max_players . A shared variable with persist is saved with the group's game, so the path is still blocked when they come back tomorrow; a different group has its own. A player's own variables are reported by the browser and can be tampered with; shared variables are held by the server, but any player's event can change them, so they are not secrets either. Both examples are in the demo: the rockfall above the spring meadow ( rockfall , shared, cleared again by the repair drone in the engine room) and the critters in the hydroponics bay ( critters_met , each player's own). Additional reserved variables: QuestLabSceneId , QuestLabPlayerName , QuestLabPlayerCount , and for the player's account QuestLabStars , QuestLabXp , QuestLabRank (the rank's name) and QuestLabAbility_ (1 while the player has a marketplace ability with that key equipped, otherwise 0). They can be used in conditions and as {{placeholders}} like any other variable. Additional condition operators: >= and <= . Items Parameter Type Default Description media_id int Image for the item. scale decimal 1.0 Display scale. blocking_radius decimal 40 Size of the obstacle for blocking items. attach_offset_x, attach_offset_y decimal 0 Where the item sits relative to the avatar's feet while worn or ridden. X is mirrored when the avatar faces left. attach_layer string front front or behind the avatar. art_faces string right Which way the artwork faces. It is mirrored to match the avatar. speed_multiplier decimal 1.5 Vehicles: walking speed while riding. Items are positioned by the bottom centre of their image, like avatars. Wearables and vehicles work the same way: clicking one within reach attaches it to the avatar, and a button on screen removes it. A player can ride one vehicle at a time. unique: true : one exists per room. While someone has it nobody else can take it, and when they let go (or disconnect) it stays where they stood, in whatever scene that is. Its position is saved with the room. unique: false : every player has their own. It disappears from the floor for the player using it and is saved with that player. blocking is implemented. physical (pushable objects) is not implemented yet . Vehicles are single objects A vehicle is always unique , whatever the document says: there is one of it in the room. It goes with whoever is riding it, across scenes. When the rider gets out it stays in that scene at that spot, where any player can climb in. Where vehicles were left is part of the room's saved data, so a vehicle left on the planet is still on the planet next lesson. Characters Parameter Type Default Description media_id int Image for the character. portrait_media_id int A close-up of the character's face, shown in the story box when they speak ( dialogue with style: "portrait" ). Without one, media_id is used. scale decimal 1.0 Display scale. A placement's event_id names an indirect event in the same scene that runs when the character is clicked, typically an infobox with what they say. Animations Sprite sheets and named animations Any image can be a sprite sheet : a grid of equal frames. The media says how the grid is cut and names the animations made of its frames. Whatever is drawn with that media (an avatar, an item, a vehicle, a character, an image_fixed picture) can then play them. Parameter Type Description sheet object { "columns": 6, "rows": 3 } : frames across and down. count may be added when the last row is not full. Frames are numbered from 0 at the top left, left to right and then down, as on the Spritemaps page. animations array { "name", "frames", "duration", "repeat" } . frames are frame numbers in the order they play. duration is the milliseconds one pass takes (default 100 per frame). repeat says whether it loops (default: by its name, see below). { "id": 120, "type": "image", "url": "avatars/sprocket-sheet.png", "sheet": { "columns": 6, "rows": 3 }, "animations": [ { "name": "idle", "frames": [0, 1], "duration": 900 }, { "name": "walk", "frames": [6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11], "duration": 600 }, { "name": "jump", "frames": [12, 13, 14, 13, 12], "duration": 600, "repeat": false }, { "name": "dance", "frames": [15, 16, 17, 16], "duration": 700 } ] } An animated PNG is not played as such. The editor reads its frames when it is uploaded and lays them out as a sprite sheet with one animation at the file's own speed, so the game has one way of animating. The existing spritemap action and spritemap labels, which describe their grid themselves, work as before. Names that mean something Name When it plays idle By itself, while the figure stands. Loops. walk By itself, while the figure moves: an avatar walking, a vehicle being ridden. Loops. It is mirrored for the direction the art does not face. walk_left , walk_right Used instead of walk for that direction, unmirrored. If only one is given, it is mirrored for the other. anything else When an animate action or a player's move asks for it. Plays once unless repeat is true ( dance loops by default). A figure with no sheet, or a sheet without idle or walk , simply stands and is mirrored to face the way it goes, as before. Built-in moves Five moves need no frames: jump (a hop), spin (a turn on the spot), crouch (a duck), wave (a sway from side to side) and dance (a looping bounce and sway). The picture itself is moved, so they work on any figure. Frames win : when a figure's sheet has an animation of the same name, that is played instead. So jump always does something, and looks best where a jump was drawn. Moves: what players can do themselves moves on the scenario lists what players can do whenever they like, from buttons on their screen. Parameter Type Description animation string The animation or built-in move to play on the player's avatar. label, icon string What the button shows. Default: the animation's name. conditions array The button is there only while these hold. Absent: always. "moves": [ { "animation": "jump" }, { "animation": "dance", "conditions": [{ "variable": "learned_dance", "operator": "=", "operand": 1 }] } ] This is the "animation inventory": a move a scenario teaches is a player's own variable set by an event, and the button appears when the condition holds. Moves of that kind belong to the scenario. Moves bought in the marketplace (shop items of kind move ) belong to the account: once bought and switched on, their buttons are there in every scenario. A pressed move plays until it ends, or for a looping one until the player walks or presses it again. Avatars differ, so a move is not tied to one avatar's art: a player whose avatar has dance frames dances with them, and any other avatar does the built-in dance. A move that is neither on the avatar's sheet nor built in does nothing for that avatar. How animations reach other players players[...].anim in the room state holds the last animation asked of a player's avatar, as name:count ; clients play it when it changes, and it is cleared when the player walks or changes scene. The server checks the name's shape and how often it is asked (four times a second at most), not whether the player "owns" the move: animations are only something to look at. Walking and standing need no message; every client works them out from the positions it already receives. Stars, XP and the marketplace Players earn stars and XP through award actions. Stars are spent in the marketplace. XP is never spent: its total decides the player's rank . Both are kept on the player's account by the backend and are the same in every scenario. Ranks Ranks are platform-wide. The defaults are in apps/api/config/qbl.php ( ranks ): XP Rank 0 Cadet 100 Explorer 300 Navigator 700 Specialist 1500 Commander 3000 Admiral What the marketplace sells Every scenario sells the platform's catalogue ( apps/api/database/seeders/data/shop.php ). A scenario can also sell items of its own, which exist only there: a mission badge, a tool for this planet. Authors add them on the editor's Shop page; they are in the document as shop_items . Parameter Type Description id int name, description string kind string wearable , pet , animation , move or ability . price int In stars. media_id int The item's picture, one of the scenario's media. (Platform items have an image_url instead.) slot string Wearables: head , body , back or hand . One item per slot is worn at a time. scale decimal Wearables and pets: height as a fraction of the avatar's height, so an item fits avatars of any size. offset_x, offset_y decimal Wearables and pets: a nudge forward and down, in avatar heights. animation string Animations: bounce , float , sway or pulse . How the avatar moves while standing. move string Moves: the animation a button on the player's screen plays, in every scenario. See Moves . ability string Abilities: a key. While equipped, QuestLabAbility_ is 1. "shop_items": [ { "id": 101, "name": "Wilting Stream patch", "kind": "wearable", "slot": "body", "price": 20, "media_id": 46, "scale": 0.14 }, { "id": 102, "name": "Stream survey map", "kind": "ability", "price": 15, "media_id": 47, "ability": "stream_map" } ] A player owns what they buy for good, and chooses what to have on: one wearable per slot, one pet, one animation (a way of standing: bounce, float, sway, pulse), and any number of moves and abilities. What a player wears is drawn on their avatar in every scenario and is seen by the other players. Abilities do nothing by themselves. They are a flag scenarios can test, so what an ability unlocks is up to each author: a hotspot only its owners see, an extra line of dialogue, a shortcut. They never change walking speed or how far away a hotspot is revealed. In the demo, the survey map makes a map table appear at the landing site: { "shortname": "survey-map", "conditions": [{ "variable": "QuestLabAbility_stream_map", "operator": "=", "operand": 1 }], "...": "..." } How it is kept honest The game client never changes stars or XP itself. When an award action runs, the client tells the game server the action's id; the game server asks the backend, which looks the action up in the published document , checks whether this player already had it, and records the change in a ledger. A player can therefore not invent an award or collect a once-only award twice. What they can do is trigger an award whose event they have not really reached, because events run in the browser (see the trust model on the protocol page). Treat stars as encouragement, not as grades. Purchases go straight from the browser to the backend, which takes the stars and hands over the item in one step. While testing a draft from the editor, awards and purchases are pretend: the preview starts with 500 stars and nothing is written to the account. Patterns These need no special support; they are combinations of the pieces above. A scored question. An indirect event holds an infobox with dismissible: false and one button per answer. Each button runs its own indirect event, which records the answer in a variable, adds to a score variable if it is the right one, and shows an infobox explaining why. A menu that stays open. An event holds a non-dismissible infobox followed by a repeat action with a condition such as menu_open = 1 . Buttons change variables or run events; a "Step away" button sets menu_open to 0, which ends the loop. Do not have an event run itself through run_event : an event that is already running is not started again. A hands-on experiment. The same loop, with buttons that change a variable ( beaker_ph + 1 ) and content that shows it ( pH {{beaker_ph}} ), plus an action whose condition detects the goal ( beaker_ph = 7 ). Collecting things. A click hotspot whose conditions include sample_x = 0 , with the object as an image label. Its actions set sample_x to 1 and add to a counter. The label disappears because the hotspot's conditions no longer hold. Not implemented yet physical items. intro_media_portrait_id / intro_media_landscape_id splash screens and is_intro_scene . allow_groups as a lobby. Groups work (players who join with the same group key share a room, up to max_players ), but choosing a group is left to whatever launches the game: pass ?group= . Animating what an avatar wears along with a sheet animation: worn items follow the figure's position, not its frames. A screen for editing the platform's marketplace catalogue and the ranks.
docs.title: Runtime extensions (spec v2)

docs.text: The original pages describe the JSON as first designed. The walk-around multiplayer runtime needs a few things those pages do not cover: where avatars can walk, where they appear, how scenes connect, where items and characters stand, and which state is shared between players. Everything on this page is optional and additive . A document that uses none of it still plays: the whole scene is walkable, players appear in the centre, and all variables are per-player. Set "spec_version": 2 on scenarios that use these fields. All coordinates are scene pixels with the origin at the top left. An avatar's position is the position of its feet .
docs.title: Runtime extensions (spec v2)

docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description spec_version int 1 Version of the spec the document was written against. code string The scenario's unique 16-letter code (lowercase a to z ). It is generated when the scenario is created, never changes, and is its address: players open /{code} . shortname stays as a readable name and can be edited freely. items array Item definitions (see Items ). Scenes place them with scenes[].items . characters array Character definitions (see Characters ). Scenes place them with scenes[].characters . asset_base_url string Prefix for media url values that are neither absolute nor rooted. A url that starts with / (such as /media/12/ab12….png , a file uploaded in the editor) is used as it is. visibility string public public : on every player's missions page. private : only for students a teacher assigned it to. chat_mode string emotes off : no chat. emotes : a fixed set of emoji only. free : typed text, filtered by the game server. move_speed decimal 420 Avatar walking speed in scene pixels per second. avatar_media_ids array Image media ids players may choose as their avatar. The first is the default. With the Laravel API these are the platform's avatars, the same in every scenario, added when the document is served (media ids from 900000); a scenario does not set them. See Classes, missions and teams . avatar_portraits object A close-up portrait for an avatar: {"<avatar media id>": <portrait media id>} . Shown when a player with that avatar speaks in a story box. An avatar without one is shown by its ordinary picture. objectives array The mission checklist shown to the player. See below. music_media_id int Background music for the scenario: it plays in every scene that does not have music of its own. music_volume decimal 0.5 Volume of that music, 0 to 1. session object null Save data for the requesting player. See Save data . jump_targets is generated from jump actions (including those on infobox buttons), by the API when it builds the JSON and again by the runtime. It may be either an object keyed by scene id ( {"3": [4]} ) or an array of {scene_id, targets} . The game server only lets a player move to a scene listed in the current scene's jump targets.
docs.title: Scenario

docs.text: A scenario can define a checklist that is shown on screen while it is played. Objectives are driven by variables, so events move the mission along simply by changing variables. Parameter Type Default Description id string or int Unique within the scenario. text string What the player reads. May contain placeholders, e.g. Collect samples ({{samples}}/3) . show_when array of conditions always The objective is listed only while these hold. Use it to reveal steps as the mission unfolds. complete_when array of conditions The objective is ticked while these hold. Required. optional bool false Shown as a bonus. The player is told when an objective becomes complete.
docs.title: Objectives

docs.text: Text overlays, infobox content, infobox button labels, text labels and objective text may contain placeholders: {{variable_name}} is replaced with the variable's current value. Reserved variables work too. {{media:ID}} is replaced with the URL of a media asset, for use in infobox HTML: . Values are escaped when inserted into HTML. A placeholder that names nothing is left as written, so a typo shows up.
docs.title: Placeholders in text

docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description width, height int first background's size World size in pixels. Set these : the game server cannot see image files, and uses the size to check movement. walkable_areas array of polygons whole scene Where feet may be. A polygon is an array of {x, y} points. A point is walkable if it is inside any of them. blocked_areas array of polygons Holes cut out of the walkable areas (furniture, pits). spawn_points array Named places players appear. See below. items array Item placements: {item_id, position_x, position_y} . characters array Character placements: {character_id, position_x, position_y, facing, event_id} . indirect_events array Events that only run via a run event action, an infobox button or a character. (Mentioned on the Events page; this is where they live.)
docs.title: Scenes

docs.text: Entries of background_media and foreground_media may be plain media objects, as before, or layer objects: Parameter Type Default Description media_id int Media to draw. position_x, position_y decimal 0 Top-left corner. display_width, display_height decimal scene size Size to draw the image at. tile bool false Repeat the image to fill the display size. scroll_speed_x, scroll_speed_y decimal 0 For tiled layers: pixels per second the texture drifts. parallax decimal 1 Camera scroll factor. 1 moves with the world, 0 stays fixed on screen. Backgrounds draw in order behind everything; foregrounds draw in order in front of avatars.
docs.title: Background and foreground layers

docs.text: A scene starts with its own music ( music_media_id , music_volume on the scene) or, failing that, the scenario's. Events can change the music at any time with an audio action flagged repeat and persist ; the next scene starts with its own music again. One music track plays at a time, and a track that is already playing is never restarted, so walking between scenes that share music is seamless. A scene whose start events start background music themselves is left to do so.
docs.title: Background music

docs.text: scale_areas is a list of boxes that give a scene depth. Whatever stands in a box is drawn at scale_top percent of its normal size at the box's top edge and scale_bottom percent at its bottom edge, and in proportion in between. It applies to avatars, to what they wear or ride, and to items and characters, by where their feet are. Parameter Type Description name string A label for the editor. x, y, width, height int The box, in scene pixels. scale_top decimal Percent of normal size at the top edge. 100 is unchanged. scale_bottom decimal Percent of normal size at the bottom edge. speed_effect decimal How much walking speed follows size, 0 to 100. Default 100: one to one, so a figure drawn at half size walks at half speed. 0: speed is unaffected. A value such as 60 lets distant figures cover ground a little faster than their size suggests without looking like they are racing. "scale_areas": [{ "name": "corridor depth", "x": 0, "y": 580, "width": 1800, "height": 620, "scale_top": 40, "scale_bottom": 100 }] Scale areas are separate from walkable areas on purpose: a crate at the far end of a room should be small even though nobody can walk there. Outside every box things are drawn at normal size. Where boxes overlap, the first one listed applies. Scale areas change how things are drawn and, through speed_effect , how fast avatars walk. Hotspot radii, reach and blocking radii stay in scene pixels. The game server's speed limit is the full walking speed, so slowing down in a scale area never conflicts with it.
docs.title: Scale areas

docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description name string Unique within the scene. The one named default is used when none is asked for. position_x, position_y decimal facing string right left or right .
docs.title: Spawn points

docs.text: Scenes are connected the way the original docs describe: with jump actions . To send players to the next scene when they reach the edge of the current one, put a walk-in hotspot along that edge and give it a jump action. A hotspot whose position_x or position_y is null covers that entire axis, so one hotspot makes a whole edge: { "id": 310, "shortname": "edge-east", "position_x": 2250, "position_y": null, "radius": 35, "activate_by_trigger": false, "actions": [{ "id": 3101, "type": "jump", "scene_id": 4, "spawn_point": "west" }] } This fires when an avatar comes within 35 pixels of x = 2250, at any height. Use position_y with a null position_x for a top or bottom edge. Because it is an ordinary hotspot it can have conditions (a locked door), and the jump can be preceded by other actions (a sound, a line of text). The scene's end events run before the jump, as always. The spawn point a jump arrives at must not be inside a walk-in hotspot that jumps, or arriving players would leave again at once. The validator rejects this.
docs.title: Moving between scenes

docs.text: activate_by_trigger keeps its meaning. In a walk-around game the two cases are: true : fires when the player clicks or taps inside the radius (or on one of the hotspot's labels). false : fires when the player's avatar walks into the radius. It fires again each time they leave and re-enter. If it cannot fire at that moment (another event is blocking hotspots, or its conditions are not met) it fires as soon as it can while the avatar is still inside. Parameter Type Default Description once bool false Fire only once per player, ever. Remembered in the save data. reveal_radius decimal The hotspot is only there when the player's avatar is within this many scene pixels of its position. Further away, its labels are invisible and it cannot be clicked. Absent: it is always there. reveal_full_radius decimal half of reveal_radius Within this distance the hotspot is fully visible. Between the two distances its labels fade in as the avatar approaches and out as it leaves. The reveal distance is measured from each player's own avatar, so a hotspot can be visible to one player and not yet to another. A coordinate the hotspot leaves empty does not count towards the distance. Walk-in hotspots still fire by their radius alone.
docs.title: Events and hotspots

docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description audience string player player : only the player who sets the event off sees it. scene : every player in the scene sees and hears it as it happens. Every kind of event can have an audience . With scene , these actions are shown to the other players in the scene at the moment they happen for the player who set the event off: audio , image_fixed , image_overlay , text_overlay , spritemap , video , dialogue , translate and cancel . In a shared dialogue, "the player" is the player who set it off: the bubble hangs over their avatar, and a story box shows their name and portrait. Everything an event does stays with the player who set it off, whatever the audience: variable , award , jump , freeze , avatar , shop , infobox and the timing actions. Nothing another player's event shows can change your variables, move you or open a box you must answer. (A variable that should change for everyone is a shared variable; see Variables . An avatar being hidden is seen by everyone anyway.) The player's own conditions decide which actions run; the others are shown exactly those. A player who walks into the scene part-way through sees the rest, not what came before. For something that must still be true for late arrivals (the boulders are across the path), use a shared variable and a hotspot or start event conditioned on it; use audience: scene for the moment itself (the boulders falling). An event run with run_event has its own audience: a private conversation can set off a shared event. The game server passes on only actions that belong to a scene event in the scene the player is in, so a player cannot push anything else onto other screens. { "id": 553, "shortname": "rockfall", "audience": "scene", "actions": [ { "type": "text_overlay", "text": "RUMBLE! Boulders crash down across the cliff path.", "duration": 3000, "blocking": false }, { "type": "variable", "name": "rockfall", "operator": "set", "operand": 1 } ] } overridable is implemented as: when any event starts, every running event flagged overridable is stopped where it is. Events not flagged always run to the end.
docs.title: Who sees an event

docs.text: Action type values are matched loosely: Image Fixed , imageFixed and image_fixed are the same. The canonical names are audio , cancel , image_fixed , image_overlay , infobox , jump , repeat , run_event , spritemap , text_overlay , translate , variable , video and wait . Actions may carry their own conditions array (the Conditions page allows this; the Actions page did not list it). An action whose conditions fail is skipped.
docs.title: Actions

docs.text: A new action type, dialogue , shows what someone says: in a speech bubble over them, or in a story box with their portrait. Parameter Type Default Description text string What is said. {{variable}} placeholders work. speaker string player player , or character . character_id int The character, when speaker is character . For a bubble it must be placed in the scene; a story box can carry a voice from anywhere. style string bubble bubble : a speech bubble over the speaker. portrait : a story box. duration int Milliseconds on screen. Absent: a bubble stays long enough to read, and a story box stays until the player continues. A click closes either sooner. { "type": "dialogue", "speaker": "character", "character_id": 1, "text": "Welcome aboard, {{QuestLabPlayerName}}!" } The bubble follows the speaker and keeps itself on screen. It sits above them when there is room, below when they are near the top of the screen, and to the right or left when there is room neither above nor below; sideways it slides along to stay inside the screen while its tail keeps pointing at the speaker. A sequence of dialogue actions is a conversation; put a freeze before it to hold the player still. The story box ( style: "portrait" ) is for the characters and moments that carry the story. It is a panel across the bottom of the screen with the speaker's close-up portrait standing on its edge, their name, and the words appearing a few at a time. The player clicks, or presses Enter or Space, to continue: once to show the whole line, again to go on. The portrait is the character's portrait_media_id (or their ordinary picture), or for the player the portrait of their avatar ( avatar_portraits ). { "type": "dialogue", "style": "portrait", "speaker": "character", "character_id": 1, "text": "Welcome aboard, {{QuestLabPlayerName}}! I am Captain Vega." } A story conversation is normally the player's own ( audience: player , the default), as the captain's greeting in the demo is. If its event is shown to the scene, the other players get a smaller version at the top of the screen that closes by itself and never takes their clicks or keys.
docs.title: Dialogue

docs.text: A new action type, animate , plays an animation on something in the scene. See Animations for where animations come from. Parameter Type Default Description animation string The animation's name: one defined on the target's sprite sheet, or a built-in move ( jump , spin , crouch , wave , dance ). Empty: stop what is playing and return to standing and walking. target string player player : the avatar of the player whose event this is. item : an item or vehicle, on the floor of this scene or being worn or ridden. character : a character placed in this scene. action : a picture that an image_fixed action is showing. item_id, character_id, target_id int Which item, character or action, for those targets. { "type": "animate", "target": "character", "character_id": 1, "animation": "wave", "blocking": false } With blocking (the default) the sequence waits until a one-pass animation has finished; a looping one never holds it up. An animation on a player's avatar goes through the game server , so everyone in the scene sees it, whatever the event's audience. An animation on an item, a character or a picture is shown to the other players only when the event's audience is scene , like anything else an event shows.
docs.title: Animate

docs.text: A new action type, freeze , stops the player from walking, or lets them walk again: for a conversation with a character, a cutscene, a countdown. Parameter Type Description frozen bool true : the player cannot move. false : they can again. { "type": "freeze", "frozen": true } A freeze ends at a freeze action with frozen: false , or when the event that froze the player finishes , or on leaving the scene, whichever comes first, so a player can never be left stuck by a missing action. While frozen a player can still click hotspots and infobox buttons. The demo freezes the player while Captain Vega is speaking.
docs.title: Freeze

docs.text: A new action type, avatar , shows or hides the player's own avatar. Parameter Type Default Description visible bool false hides the avatar, true shows it. duration int 0 Fade time in milliseconds. { "type": "avatar", "visible": false, "duration": 400 } The change goes through the game server, so every player in the scene sees it. A hidden player can still walk and use hotspots. Avatars are always shown again when a player arrives in a scene : to keep them hidden in a scene, hide them in one of its start events. The demo's rocket hides the avatar as the player steps aboard, and the player reappears in the control room. (The scene attribute show_avatars: false from the base docs still hides every avatar in a scene, for everyone, for the whole visit.)
docs.title: Avatar

docs.text: A new action type, award , gives the player stars, XP, or both. A negative number takes them away. Parameter Type Default Description stars int 0 Stars to give (or take, if negative). Stars are the currency of the marketplace. xp int 0 Experience points to give (or take). XP is never spent; it adds up to a rank. note string A few words shown with the award: "Sample collected". repeatable bool false By default a player gets each award once , however often its event runs and in however many visits. Set this to give it every time. { "type": "award", "stars": 3, "xp": 10, "note": "Sample collected" } Stars and XP belong to the player's account , not to a scenario: they carry across every scenario on the platform. See Stars, XP and the marketplace for how they are kept honest. Neither total goes below zero. Taking away more than a player has leaves them with none. Guests earn nothing. Stars and XP need a signed-in account. Put awards in an event's own actions. An award placed directly on an infobox button is not given (the validator warns): make the button run an event ( run_event ) that contains the award. Awards never hold up the sequence, whatever blocking says.
docs.title: Award

docs.text: A new action type, shop , opens the marketplace. It has no parameters. The sequence waits until the player closes the window. { "type": "shop" } Players can also open the marketplace at any time from the stars shown in the corner of the screen, so a scenario needs no shop action; it is there for scenarios that want a place for it, as the demo's marketplace room does. Addition Applies to Description dismissible infobox Default true. See below. spawn_point jump Spawn point to arrive at in the target scene. target_event_id run_event The event to run. Use this rather than event_id , which the base action attributes already use for "the event this action belongs to". event_id is still read if target_event_id is absent. layer image_fixed, spritemap above (default) draws over avatars and foregrounds. sorted depth-sorts with avatars using position_y , so players can walk in front of it. position_x, position_y, scale_x, scale_y, alpha, duration translate Values present are animated on the target over duration milliseconds. Position applies to image_fixed and spritemap targets; overlays support scale and alpha. alignment, scale_x, scale_y, volume video Video plays as an overlay with browser controls. It blocks until it ends. Clarifications of documented behaviour: An action with no end (an image or text with duration 0, repeating audio, a repeating spritemap) never holds up the sequence, whatever blocking says. It stays until a cancel or a jump. A repeat with no wait in its loop runs about once per frame rather than freezing the page. call_to_actions is a list of {"text": "...", "action": {...}, "conditions": [...]} . The action needs no id . A button with conditions is only offered while they hold, so one infobox can serve as a menu that changes. An infobox has a close button unless dismissible is false . A box that cannot be dismissed must be answered with one of its buttons, which is how questions are asked. An infobox action is not finished until the box is closed and the chosen button's action has run to its end. A sequence such as "ask a question, then open a menu" therefore waits for the feedback the answer triggers. Infobox content is sanitised. Formatting, lists, tables, links and images are kept; scripts, styles, frames and event handlers are removed. Background music is an audio action with repeat and persist in a scene's start events. Persistent audio is treated as the music track: only one plays at a time. When a scene starts a persistent audio action with the same media that is already playing, the music carries on without restarting; with different media, it replaces the old track. A cancel action naming the audio action's id stops it.
docs.title: Shop

docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description scope string player player : each player has their own value, saved with their progress. room : one value shared by everyone in the group, held by the game server. persist bool true If false the variable returns to default_value on every visit. Each variable is one or the other, and its scope says which. A player's own variable ( player ) has a separate value for every player. Changing it for one player changes nothing for anyone else. Use it for a player's progress: students must greet three animals before a door opens, and each has their own count of how many they have greeted. A shared variable ( room ) has one value for everyone playing together. When any player changes it, it changes for all of them at once, wherever in the scenario they are. Use it for the state of the world: one student sends boulders down across a path, and after that nobody can use the path. Conditions and variable actions are written the same way for both; only the variable's scope differs, so a scenario decides this once, where the variable is defined, and not in every action. A variable action on a shared variable is sent to the game server, applied there, and the new value reaches every player; hotspots and objectives whose conditions use it update for everyone. The editor marks shared variables wherever one is chosen. "Everyone playing together" is a group: the players who joined with the same group key (a class, a team), up to max_players . A shared variable with persist is saved with the group's game, so the path is still blocked when they come back tomorrow; a different group has its own. A player's own variables are reported by the browser and can be tampered with; shared variables are held by the server, but any player's event can change them, so they are not secrets either. Both examples are in the demo: the rockfall above the spring meadow ( rockfall , shared, cleared again by the repair drone in the engine room) and the critters in the hydroponics bay ( critters_met , each player's own). Additional reserved variables: QuestLabSceneId , QuestLabPlayerName , QuestLabPlayerCount , and for the player's account QuestLabStars , QuestLabXp , QuestLabRank (the rank's name) and QuestLabAbility_<key> (1 while the player has a marketplace ability with that key equipped, otherwise 0). They can be used in conditions and as {{placeholders}} like any other variable. Additional condition operators: >= and <= .
docs.title: Variables

docs.text: Parameter Type Default Description media_id int Image for the item. scale decimal 1.0 Display scale. blocking_radius decimal 40 Size of the obstacle for blocking items. attach_offset_x, attach_offset_y decimal 0 Where the item sits relative to the avatar's feet while worn or ridden. X is mirrored when the avatar faces left. attach_layer string front front or behind the avatar. art_faces string right Which way the artwork faces. It is mirrored to match the avatar. speed_multiplier decimal 1.5 Vehicles: walking speed while riding. Items are positioned by the bottom centre of their image, like avatars. Wearables and vehicles work the same way: clicking one within reach attaches it to the avatar, and a button on screen removes it. A player can ride one vehicle at a time. unique: true : one exists per room. While someone has it nobody else can take it, and when they let go (or disconnect) it stays where they stood, in whatever scene that is. Its position is saved with the room. unique: false : every player has their own. It disappears from the floor for the player using it and is saved with that player. blocking is implemented. physical (pushable objects) is not implemented yet .
docs.title: Items

docs.text: A vehicle is always unique , whatever the document says: there is one of it in the room. It goes with whoever is riding it, across scenes. When the rider gets out it stays in that scene at that spot, where any player can climb in. Where vehicles were left is part of the room's saved data, so a vehicle left on the planet is still on the planet next lesson.
docs.title: Vehicles are single objects

Without one, media_id is used. scale decimal 1.0 Display scale. A placement's event_id names an indirect event in the same scene that runs when the character is clicked, typically an infobox with what they say.

docs.text: Any image can be a sprite sheet : a grid of equal frames. The media says how the grid is cut and names the animations made of its frames. Whatever is drawn with that media (an avatar, an item, a vehicle, a character, an image_fixed picture) can then play them. Parameter Type Description sheet object { "columns": 6, "rows": 3 } : frames across and down. count may be added when the last row is not full. Frames are numbered from 0 at the top left, left to right and then down, as on the Spritemaps page. animations array { "name", "frames", "duration", "repeat" } . frames are frame numbers in the order they play. duration is the milliseconds one pass takes (default 100 per frame). repeat says whether it loops (default: by its name, see below). { "id": 120, "type": "image", "url": "avatars/sprocket-sheet.png", "sheet": { "columns": 6, "rows": 3 }, "animations": [ { "name": "idle", "frames": [0, 1], "duration": 900 }, { "name": "walk", "frames": [6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11], "duration": 600 }, { "name": "jump", "frames": [12, 13, 14, 13, 12], "duration": 600, "repeat": false }, { "name": "dance", "frames": [15, 16, 17, 16], "duration": 700 } ] } An animated PNG is not played as such. The editor reads its frames when it is uploaded and lays them out as a sprite sheet with one animation at the file's own speed, so the game has one way of animating. The existing spritemap action and spritemap labels, which describe their grid themselves, work as before.
docs.title: Sprite sheets and named animations

docs.text: Name When it plays idle By itself, while the figure stands. Loops. walk By itself, while the figure moves: an avatar walking, a vehicle being ridden. Loops. It is mirrored for the direction the art does not face. walk_left , walk_right Used instead of walk for that direction, unmirrored. If only one is given, it is mirrored for the other. anything else When an animate action or a player's move asks for it. Plays once unless repeat is true ( dance loops by default). A figure with no sheet, or a sheet without idle or walk , simply stands and is mirrored to face the way it goes, as before.
docs.title: Names that mean something

docs.text: Five moves need no frames: jump (a hop), spin (a turn on the spot), crouch (a duck), wave (a sway from side to side) and dance (a looping bounce and sway). The picture itself is moved, so they work on any figure. Frames win : when a figure's sheet has an animation of the same name, that is played instead. So jump always does something, and looks best where a jump was drawn.
docs.title: Built-in moves

docs.text: moves on the scenario lists what players can do whenever they like, from buttons on their screen. Parameter Type Description animation string The animation or built-in move to play on the player's avatar. label, icon string What the button shows. Default: the animation's name. conditions array The button is there only while these hold. Absent: always. "moves": [ { "animation": "jump" }, { "animation": "dance", "conditions": [{ "variable": "learned_dance", "operator": "=", "operand": 1 }] } ] This is the "animation inventory": a move a scenario teaches is a player's own variable set by an event, and the button appears when the condition holds. Moves of that kind belong to the scenario. Moves bought in the marketplace (shop items of kind move ) belong to the account: once bought and switched on, their buttons are there in every scenario. A pressed move plays until it ends, or for a looping one until the player walks or presses it again. Avatars differ, so a move is not tied to one avatar's art: a player whose avatar has dance frames dances with them, and any other avatar does the built-in dance. A move that is neither on the avatar's sheet nor built in does nothing for that avatar.
docs.title: Moves: what players can do themselves

docs.text: players[...].anim in the room state holds the last animation asked of a player's avatar, as name:count ; clients play it when it changes, and it is cleared when the player walks or changes scene. The server checks the name's shape and how often it is asked (four times a second at most), not whether the player "owns" the move: animations are only something to look at. Walking and standing need no message; every client works them out from the positions it already receives.

docs.text: Players earn stars and XP through award actions. Stars are spent in the marketplace. XP is never spent: its total decides the player's rank . Both are kept on the player's account by the backend and are the same in every scenario.

docs.text: Every scenario sells the platform's catalogue ( apps/api/database/seeders/data/shop.php ). A scenario can also sell items of its own, which exist only there: a mission badge, a tool for this planet. Authors add them on the editor's Shop page; they are in the document as shop_items . Parameter Type Description id int name, description string kind string wearable , pet , animation , move or ability . price int In stars. media_id int The item's picture, one of the scenario's media. (Platform items have an image_url instead.) slot string Wearables: head , body , back or hand . One item per slot is worn at a time. scale decimal Wearables and pets: height as a fraction of the avatar's height, so an item fits avatars of any size. offset_x, offset_y decimal Wearables and pets: a nudge forward and down, in avatar heights. animation string Animations: bounce , float , sway or pulse . How the avatar moves while standing. move string Moves: the animation a button on the player's screen plays, in every scenario. See Moves . ability string Abilities: a key. While equipped, QuestLabAbility_<key> is 1. "shop_items": [ { "id": 101, "name": "Wilting Stream patch", "kind": "wearable", "slot": "body", "price": 20, "media_id": 46, "scale": 0.14 }, { "id": 102, "name": "Stream survey map", "kind": "ability", "price": 15, "media_id": 47, "ability": "stream_map" } ] A player owns what they buy for good, and chooses what to have on: one wearable per slot, one pet, one animation (a way of standing: bounce, float, sway, pulse), and any number of moves and abilities. What a player wears is drawn on their avatar in every scenario and is seen by the other players. Abilities do nothing by themselves. They are a flag scenarios can test, so what an ability unlocks is up to each author: a hotspot only its owners see, an extra line of dialogue, a shortcut. They never change walking speed or how far away a hotspot is revealed. In the demo, the survey map makes a map table appear at the landing site: { "shortname": "survey-map", "conditions": [{ "variable": "QuestLabAbility_stream_map", "operator": "=", "operand": 1 }], "...": "..." }

docs.text: The game client never changes stars or XP itself. When an award action runs, the client tells the game server the action's id; the game server asks the backend, which looks the action up in the published document , checks whether this player already had it, and records the change in a ledger. A player can therefore not invent an award or collect a once-only award twice. What they can do is trigger an award whose event they have not really reached, because events run in the browser (see the trust model on the protocol page). Treat stars as encouragement, not as grades. Purchases go straight from the browser to the backend, which takes the stars and hands over the item in one step. While testing a draft from the editor, awards and purchases are pretend: the preview starts with 500 stars and nothing is written to the account.
docs.title: How it is kept honest

docs.text: These need no special support; they are combinations of the pieces above. A scored question. An indirect event holds an infobox with dismissible: false and one button per answer. Each button runs its own indirect event, which records the answer in a variable, adds to a score variable if it is the right one, and shows an infobox explaining why. A menu that stays open. An event holds a non-dismissible infobox followed by a repeat action with a condition such as menu_open = 1 . Buttons change variables or run events; a "Step away" button sets menu_open to 0, which ends the loop. Do not have an event run itself through run_event : an event that is already running is not started again. A hands-on experiment. The same loop, with buttons that change a variable ( beaker_ph + 1 ) and content that shows it ( pH {{beaker_ph}} ), plus an action whose condition detects the goal ( beaker_ph = 7 ). Collecting things. A click hotspot whose conditions include sample_x = 0 , with the object as an image label. Its actions set sample_x to 1 and add to a counter. The label disappears because the hotspot's conditions no longer hold.
docs.title: Patterns

docs.text: Multiplayer protocol The client joins a Colyseus room named scenario . Rooms are matched on scenario and group , so players who launch the same scenario with the same group key share a room, whichever scene each of them is in. The types live in packages/shared/src/protocol.ts . Join options Option Description scenario Scenario shortname. group Group key. Defaults to public . token API bearer token. Required. avatar_media_id Chosen avatar; must be in the scenario's avatar_media_ids . If absent, the avatar saved on the account is used. If the same account joins twice, the earlier connection is closed with code 4103. Synchronized state State the server owns and every client sees (Colyseus schema, apps/server/src/rooms/state.ts ): players[sessionId] : user_id , name , role , avatar , scene_id , x , y , facing , attachments (comma-separated item ids), connected , hidden (an avatar action has hidden this player; cleared on every scene change), anim (the last animation asked of the avatar, as name:count ; cleared when the player walks or changes scene), look (comma-separated ids of the marketplace items the player has on; the server reads it from the backend, never from the client). items[itemId] : unique items only. scene_id , x , y , holder (a session id, or empty). vars[name] : room-scoped variables, JSON-encoded. Clients draw the players whose scene_id matches their own. Client to server Message Payload Server behaviour move {x, y, facing} Accepted if the spot is walkable and within the distance the avatar could have covered. Otherwise the server replies snap . scene {scene_id, spawn_point?} Accepted if the scene is a jump target of the current one. The player is placed on the spawn point. var {name, operator, operand?} Applies a variable action to a room-scoped variable. item {item_id, action: "attach" or "detach"} Checks reach, uniqueness and the one-vehicle rule. emote {emoji} Must be in the allowed list; rate limited. Not available when chat_mode is off . chat {text} Only when chat_mode is free . Cleaned, length-limited and rate limited. progress {variables, flags, time_elapsed} Player-scoped progress to include in the next save. avatar {visible} An avatar action ran: show or hide the sender's avatar for everyone in the scene. award {action_id} An award action ran. The server asks the backend to grant it and replies progress . Ignored for guests. animate {name} Play an animation on the sender's avatar, from a move button or an animate action. The name must look like a name; at most four a second. An empty name stops it. show {event_id, action_id} An event whose audience is scene reached this action for the sender. Passed on to the other players in the sender's scene if the action belongs to such an event there and is one of the shown types. look {} The player changed what they wear. The server fetches their look from the backend and updates players[...].look . Server to client Message Payload Meaning welcome {session_id, session, chat_mode} Sent on join with the save data to start from. snap {x, y, scene_id} A move was refused; return to this position. chat {session_id, text} emote {session_id, emoji} notice {code, message} Something to tell the player, e.g. an item is taken. show {session_id, event_id, action_id} Another player's event is showing this action. The client presents it and changes nothing else. progress {stars, xp, rank, next_rank_xp, owned, equipped, delta_stars, delta_xp, note?, rank_up?} The result of an award: the player's new totals and what changed. Trust model The client predicts its own movement and runs scene events locally, because events are presentation (sounds, pictures, text) and each player experiences them individually. The server decides everything players could otherwise cheat on or disagree about: positions, which scene a player is in, who holds a unique item, shared variable values, what is saved, and stars and XP (an award is granted by the backend from the published document, once per player unless it repeats). Player-scoped variables are reported by the client and are therefore not tamper-proof ; treat them as progress markers, not as grades. Reconnection A dropped connection keeps its seat for 30 seconds ( QuestLab_RECONNECT_SECONDS ). The avatar is shown faded to others meanwhile. The SDK reconnects by itself.

A scenario is composed of multiple scenes, and scenes contain events which describe interactions within the scene. docs.text: Save data When enable_save_session is true, a player's progress is saved and delivered with the scenario the next time they visit, as the session object at the top level of the scenario JSON. Parameter Type Description scene_id int The scene the player was in. position_x, position_y decimal Where they stood. If that spot is no longer walkable (the scene was edited), the nearest walkable point is used. If the scene no longer exists, they start at start_scene_id . variables object Values of player-scoped variables with persist not false, by name. attachments array Ids of non-unique items the player was wearing or riding. flags array One-shot markers, such as hotspot:420 for a hotspot flagged once that has fired. time_elapsed int Total seconds spent in the scenario. Feeds QuestLabTimeElapsed . updated_at string ISO 8601 time of the save. "session": { "scene_id": 2, "position_x": 1050, "position_y": 1000, "variables": { "mission": "flora", "visited_ship": 1 }, "attachments": [2], "flags": ["hotspot:420"], "time_elapsed": 734, "updated_at": "2026-11-15T17:37:00.000Z" } Who writes it The game server. It knows where each player is and what they hold; the client reports its player-scoped variables and flags every few seconds and before each jump. Saves happen when a player leaves or drops, and periodically while they play. Values reported by the client are filtered: only variables declared in global_variables with player scope are kept. Room data State shared by a group is saved separately, per scenario and group key: Parameter Type Description variables object Values of room-scoped variables with persist not false. items object For each unique item id: {scene_id, x, y} , where it was left. It is loaded when the first player of a group arrives and saved when the room empties and whenever it changes. It is not part of the scenario JSON; clients receive it through the live room state.

docs.text: Spritemaps A spritemap is an animation that can be used in a label or as an action. A PNG containing all the frames for an animation shown together, called a sprite sheet, is referenced by the spritemap to produce the animation. A single sprite sheet can be used for multiple animations. In fact, this is preferred, so only one image has to be retrieved for all animations for a particular object or character. Each time a spritemap action is executed, it contains extra details about how to interpret the sprite sheet.
